title: Inverse Circular Functions
notes: ### 1. Why a principal branch is needed
Sine, cosine, and tangent are not one-to-one on all real numbers, so each inverse is defined only on a chosen branch. sin⁻¹x is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is x, for x in [−1, 1].
cos⁻¹x lies in [0, π]. tan⁻¹x lies in (−π/2, π/2). The principal value is the unique answer inside that range, so a positive ratio does not by itself decide the sign.
sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 for x in [−1, 1]. tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2 for real x. Both angles in each pair sit inside their principal ranges and add to a right angle.
tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x+y)/(1−xy)) when xy < 1. If x > 0, y > 0, and xy > 1, the sum of the two principal values is greater than π/2, so add π to the tan⁻¹ of (x+y)/(1−xy).
tan⁻¹(1) = π/4 and tan⁻¹(2) is positive, so their sum is greater than π/2. The formula tan⁻¹((1+2)/(1−2)) = tan⁻¹(−3) is the wrong branch, because the product xy = 2 is greater than 1.

keyPoints: The principal-value range of each inverse decides the sign of the answer — substituting a positive ratio into cos⁻¹ gives an angle in [0, π], never a negative one.
